crime: Every evening a girl skipped stones on the lake shore. She alone accepted every gift from {WITCH_NAME}, laughing each time. At dusk she lay back on the shingle to count the stars.

Each dusk {WITCH_NAME} handed her a pebble, and as it reached her hand it became what she needed most just then: a shawl, a lantern, never what {WITCH_NAME} expected. Girls walking back along the shore stopped to watch it change.

One evening, for once, {WITCH_NAME} picked a flat stone herself and handed it over. It stayed a stone in the girl's hand. "Your magic's off tonight," the girl laughed. She skipped it away without a look and held out her hand for another.
At nine, {WITCH_NAME} had chosen a snow globe herself for her only friend's birthday. The next morning she saw it in the classroom bin. Whatever she chose herself got thrown away.
As the girl bent in the shallows for another, {WITCH_NAME} picked up a stone from the shore and struck her temple. The girl dropped onto the shingle.

At dusk, as the girls on the shore watched, {WITCH_NAME} knelt and closed a pebble in the girl's limp hand. It turned into a small roll of pale cloth. Then she walked back with them and stayed in their sight until the body was found.
Before lockup, the girl's roommate went down and found her cold on the shingle, her temple broken, the roll still in her fingers.
In the trial court, the prisoners ruled: "The gift changed in her hand, so she was alive when {WITCH_NAME} left. Some girl struck her dead after dusk, while {WITCH_NAME} sat with us."
Then a prisoner unrolled the gift from the dead girl's fingers. It was a head bandage. She had no other wound.
The prisoners understood. The pebble had become what she needed most right then. Her temple was already broken when {WITCH_NAME} knelt beside her.
fields.epitaph: The one time she knew exactly what someone needed, nothing changed, and no one saw.
fields.epithet: The Giver Whose Gifts Choose Themselves
execution: The execution stand raises a wire wastebin around her, the kind that sits in every classroom, its walls as high as the trial court's own. She stands alone on its floor. Far above, a great snow globe balances on its rim.
The globe tips over the rim and drops into the bin, onto her upraised open hands. It stays a snow globe all the way down.
It comes to rest upright on the floor of the bin. Through the wire, snow still drifts inside it, and one open hand lies beneath its base.

magic.name: Just What You Needed
magic.text: Any object she hands someone becomes what they need most right now as it reaches their hand.
